title: Biogenic N-Doped Carbon Quantum Dots for Fluorescent Iron Sensing in Environmental Systems: Synthesis, Mechanistic Elucidation, and Phytotoxicity Assessment
content: Biomass-derived fluorescent carbon nanomaterials offer opportunities for sensing applications, provided their optical performance, stability, and biological compatibility are adequately evaluated. Here, nitrogen-doped carbon quantum dots (NCQDs) were prepared from Pogostemon benghalensis leaves by a one-step hydrothermal method using ethylenediamine as the nitrogen source. Spectroscopic and microscopic characterization revealed blue-emitting NCQDs with a fluorescence quantum yield of 15.53% and good aqueous dispersibility. Their fluorescence remained stable across the tested pH and ionic-strength ranges, during prolonged UV irradiation, and upon storage. Quenching by Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺ was investigated using UV–visible absorption spectroscopy, time-resolved photoluminescence, Stern–Volmer analysis, and zeta-potential measurements. The results supported predominantly static quenching associated with ground-state complex formation, with a possible contribution from photoinduced electron transfer. In separate assays, the NCQDs detected Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺ with detection limits of 0.061 and 0.067 μM, respectively. Their analytical applicability was evaluated in tap water, river water, soil extracts, and pharmaceutical samples. Seed-germination experiments with Vigna radiata showed 100% germination at NCQD concentrations up to 10 ppm, while concentrations of 3–6 ppm accelerated early germination under the tested conditions. These findings support the potential of leaf-derived NCQDs as fluorescent probes for iron analysis and indicate compatibility with Vigna radiata germination at the concentrations examined.
